RagShortTexts: In 1266 at Benevento, Charles of Anjou slew King Manfred, replacing Hohenstaufen rule with.

Variants.Content: Charles of Anjou brought an army into southern Italy in 1265 with papal backing, and his campaign against the Hohenstaufen kingdom reached its climax at Benevento on February 26, 1266. The battle was fought along the Calore River, where Manfred of Sicily commanded the royal army. Charles's French knights pressed the Sicilian lines, and when the Italian baronial contingents on Manfred's side gave way, the king threw himself into the melee and died there. The fight ended Hohenstaufen rule over the kingdom of Sicily. Angevin control then depended on garrisons in the towns and on the taxes the new regime could collect. The battle also showed how quickly a feudal army could fall apart once its commander's own vassals began to abandon him.

After Benevento, a lord in Naples or Sicily had to decide quickly whether to swear to the new Angevin rulers. Those who had backed Manfred risked confiscation, while those who switched sides kept their fiefs by paying the right fines. Letters from the papal curia and the new court moved faster than any messenger from the old house.
